title: SYSK Selects: Whatever happened to acid rain?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of "Whatever Happened to Acid Rain?" (originally 2012). Josh introduces the episode as a Selects pick. The hosts explain acid rain as a transboundary problem caused by sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions that form sulfuric and nitric acid, wet and dry acid deposition, and the pH scale (normal rain about 5.6). They cover ecosystem effects: plankton and food chain collapse, coastal algae blooms from nitrogen, soil buffering overload and aluminum leaching harming trees, forest bald peaks from acid fog, and health and material damage such as smog-related respiratory problems and corroded stone and car paint. History covered: Robert Angus Smith coined "acid rain" in 1872, the 1980 Acid Deposition Act, the 1990 Clean Air Act amendments, and the cap-and-trade system for sulfur dioxide, which cut emissions sharply, plus a later nitrogen oxide cap-and-trade from 2003 and reductions in acidic lakes in Wisconsin, Michigan, and the Adirondacks. The episode closes with a listener mail segment from an MIT student correcting the "eggheads" reference (MIT Engineers, Tim the Beaver, Course 24 linguistics), and a request for listeners to explain "chocolate rain".

entities.name: Clean Air Status and Trends Network

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects episode on acid rain from 2012 and the hosts banter about John Denver-style music, the 1980s environmental worries, and the ozone layer.

segments.title: What acid rain is and the pH scale
segments.summary: Acid rain is defined as rain with acid from sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions, which form sulfuric and nitric acid. It includes wet and dry acid deposition. The hosts explain the pH scale, neutral water at 7, and normal rain at about 5.6 due to carbonic acid.

segments.title: Effects on ecosystems: plankton, soil, and monitoring
segments.summary: Acidity harms plankton and small invertebrates, cascading up the food chain. Monitoring programs measure hydrogen ion concentration and critical loads. Soil buffering can be overloaded, passing acid into water bodies.

segments.title: Coastal algae blooms, aluminum, and forest damage
segments.summary: Nitrogen from nitric acid fuels algae blooms, which lead to oxygen depletion in coastal waters. Acid rain draws aluminum from soil that harms trees, and acid fog at high elevations strips leaves, causing bald peaks in the Appalachians.

segments.title: Human health and material damage
segments.summary: Acid rain is less harmful to people directly, but dry deposition combined with ozone can form smog that harms the respiratory system. Acid also corrodes stone monuments and car paint.

segments.title: History: Robert Angus Smith and early discovery
segments.summary: Robert Angus Smith coined the term acid rain in 1872 after noticing damage to monuments. The hosts note the problem was thought local until the 1970s and 1980s, and reflect on industrial revolution priorities.

segments.title: Policy success: Acid Deposition Act, Clean Air Act, cap and trade
segments.summary: The 1980 Acid Deposition Act led to a ten-year study, and the 1990 amendments added sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides to the Clean Air Act. A cap-and-trade system cut sulfur dioxide emissions sharply, and a nitrogen oxide cap-and-trade came in 2003. Acidic lakes in Wisconsin, Michigan, and the Adirondacks declined.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: The episode ends with listener mail and an MIT student's correction to the 'eggheads' reference, and a request for listeners to explain chocolate rain.
